facts.summary: Minnesota's minimum wage is $11.41 per hour for all employers effective January 1, 2026 (adjusted annually for inflation), higher than the federal $7.25.
facts.sourceAgency: Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry
facts.notes: Effective Jan. 1, 2026. A 90-day training wage of $9.31 applies to workers under age 20. Minneapolis and St. Paul have separate, higher local minimum-wage ordinances.

facts.value: no overtime protection beyond federal FLSA (Minnesota's own 48-hr/week threshold is weaker than the federal 40-hr rule)
facts.summary: Minnesota's own overtime statute requires time-and-a-half only after 48 hours in a workweek -- a weaker threshold than the federal FLSA's 40 hours. Because nearly all employers are also covered by the FLSA, the federal 40-hour rule is the one that actually applies in practice, so state law adds no extra overtime protection beyond what federal law already requires. There is no daily overtime under Minnesota law.
facts.sourceAgency: Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry
facts.notes: Confirmed 2026-08-08 against revisor.mn.gov statute text and dli.mn.gov guidance: the 48-hour state threshold is LESS protective than the FLSA's 40-hour threshold, so it functions as a floor only for the small minority of MN-only employers not reached by the FLSA. No daily OT under state law. This fact should never be treated as an 'extra protection beyond federal' state for wage-letter purposes.

value: status with regard to public assistance
facts.summary: The Minnesota Human Rights Act protects more classes than federal law, adding creed, marital status, familial status, sexual orientation, gender identity, and status with regard to public assistance.
facts.notes: Race definition includes traits associated with race such as hair texture and hairstyle. Verify full current class list against 363A.03 definitions.

facts.summary: The Minnesota Human Rights Act covers any employer with one or more employees, far broader than the federal 15-employee threshold under Title VII/ADA.
facts.sourceAgency: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
facts.notes: 'Employer' means a person who has one or more employees.

facts.value: 18 and older (no upper or lower age floor of 40)
facts.summary: The Minnesota Human Rights Act protects workers 18 and older from age discrimination, broader than the federal ADEA which only protects workers 40 and older.
facts.notes: Unlike federal ADEA (20+ employees, age 40+), MHRA age protection is not limited to workers over 40. Confirm exact age-definition wording in 363A.03.

facts.value: Minnesota Whistleblower Act prohibits retaliation for good-faith reports of legal violations
facts.summary: The Minnesota Whistleblower Act bars employers from retaliating against employees who in good faith report suspected legal violations, participate in investigations, or refuse to perform illegal acts.
facts.sourceAgency: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
facts.notes: Protects good-faith reports; false statements or reckless disregard for the truth are not protected. This is a state-law addition to federal protections.

facts.summary: A wage or overtime claim in Minnesota must generally be brought within two years, extended to three years where nonpayment is willful or the employer fails to produce payroll records.
facts.sourceAgency: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
facts.notes: Two-year default; three years for willful nonpayment or failure to submit payroll records to DLI on request.

facts.summary: A charge of discrimination under the Minnesota Human Rights Act must be filed with the Department of Human Rights within one year of the discriminatory act, longer than the federal EEOC 180/300-day deadlines.
facts.notes: One year from the date discrimination occurred. Verify the exact statutory subdivision citation (363A.28, subd. 3) against current statute.

facts.summary: Minnesota voids employee non-compete agreements: any covenant not to compete contained in a contract or agreement is void and unenforceable, with narrow exceptions for agreements made in connection with the sale of a business or in anticipation of dissolving a partnership, LLC, or corporation. The ban applies to covenants entered into on or after July 1, 2023 (agreements from before that date are analyzed under prior common law). Non-solicitation and confidentiality/trade-secret agreements are separately defined and are not automatically void.
facts.sourceAgency: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against primary statute text (subd. 1-2). A court may award a prevailing employee reasonable attorney fees in addition to injunctive relief and other remedies. The law also restricts choice-of-law/venue clauses that would apply another state's law or require litigation outside Minnesota for a Minnesota employee (subd. 3).

facts.value: Discharge: due within 24 hours of demand; resignation: next payday (or within 20 days)
facts.summary: Minnesota requires final wages of a discharged employee within 24 hours of demand, and a resigning employee's final wages by the next regular payday, with penalty wages up to 15 days for noncompliance.
facts.sourceAgency: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
facts.notes: 181.13 governs discharge (immediate/within 24 hrs of demand); 181.14 governs resignation (next payday, generally within 20 days). Federal law has no such final-pay timing rule.
